search_paper_list.title:
Predicated Diffusion: Predicate Logic-Based Attention Guidance for
  Text-to-Image Diffusion Models
search_paper_list.summary:
Diffusion models have achieved remarkable results in generating high-quality,
diverse, and creative images. However, when it comes to text-based image
generation, they often fail to capture the intended meaning presented in the
text. For instance, a specified object may not be generated, an unnecessary
object may be generated, and an adjective may alter objects it was not intended
to modify. Moreover, we found that relationships indicating possession between
objects are often overlooked. While users' intentions in text are diverse,
existing methods tend to specialize in only some aspects of these. In this
paper, we propose Predicated Diffusion, a unified framework to express users'
intentions. We consider that the root of the above issues lies in the text
encoder, which often focuses only on individual words and neglects the logical
relationships between them. The proposed method does not solely rely on the
text encoder, but instead, represents the intended meaning in the text as
propositions using predicate logic and treats the pixels in the attention maps
as the fuzzy predicates. This enables us to obtain a differentiable loss
function that makes the image fulfill the proposition by minimizing it. When
compared to several existing methods, we demonstrated that Predicated Diffusion
can generate images that are more faithful to various text prompts, as verified
by human evaluators and pretrained image-text models.

search_paper_list.title:
Morphological Prototyping for Unsupervised Slide Representation Learning
  in Computational Pathology
search_paper_list.summary:
Representation learning of pathology whole-slide images (WSIs) has been has
primarily relied on weak supervision with Multiple Instance Learning (MIL).
However, the slide representations resulting from this approach are highly
tailored to specific clinical tasks, which limits their expressivity and
generalization, particularly in scenarios with limited data. Instead, we
hypothesize that morphological redundancy in tissue can be leveraged to build a
task-agnostic slide representation in an unsupervised fashion. To this end, we
introduce PANTHER, a prototype-based approach rooted in the Gaussian mixture
model that summarizes the set of WSI patches into a much smaller set of
morphological prototypes. Specifically, each patch is assumed to have been
generated from a mixture distribution, where each mixture component represents
a morphological exemplar. Utilizing the estimated mixture parameters, we then
construct a compact slide representation that can be readily used for a wide
range of downstream tasks. By performing an extensive evaluation of PANTHER on
subtyping and survival tasks using 13 datasets, we show that 1) PANTHER
outperforms or is on par with supervised MIL baselines and 2) the analysis of
morphological prototypes brings new qualitative and quantitative insights into
model interpretability.

search_paper_list.title:
Deep Learning-enabled Virtual Histological Staining of Biological
  Samples
search_paper_list.summary:
Histological staining is the gold standard for tissue examination in clinical
pathology and life-science research, which visualizes the tissue and cellular
structures using chromatic dyes or fluorescence labels to aid the microscopic
assessment of tissue. However, the current histological staining workflow
requires tedious sample preparation steps, specialized laboratory
infrastructure, and trained histotechnologists, making it expensive,
time-consuming, and not accessible in resource-limited settings. Deep learning
techniques created new opportunities to revolutionize staining methods by
digitally generating histological stains using trained neural networks,
providing rapid, cost-effective, and accurate alternatives to standard chemical
staining methods. These techniques, broadly referred to as virtual staining,
were extensively explored by multiple research groups and demonstrated to be
successful in generating various types of histological stains from label-free
microscopic images of unstained samples; similar approaches were also used for
transforming images of an already stained tissue sample into another type of
stain, performing virtual stain-to-stain transformations. In this Review, we
provide a comprehensive overview of the recent research advances in deep
learning-enabled virtual histological staining techniques. The basic concepts
and the typical workflow of virtual staining are introduced, followed by a
discussion of representative works and their technical innovations. We also
share our perspectives on the future of this emerging field, aiming to inspire
readers from diverse scientific fields to further expand the scope of deep
learning-enabled virtual histological staining techniques and their
applications.

search_paper_list.title:
GLiDR: Topologically Regularized Graph Generative Network for Sparse
  LiDAR Point Clouds
search_paper_list.summary:
Sparse LiDAR point clouds cause severe loss of detail of static structures
and reduce the density of static points available for navigation. Reduced
density can be detrimental to navigation under several scenarios. We observe
that despite high sparsity, in most cases, the global topology of LiDAR
outlining the static structures can be inferred. We utilize this property to
obtain a backbone skeleton of a LiDAR scan in the form of a single connected
component that is a proxy to its global topology. We utilize the backbone to
augment new points along static structures to overcome sparsity. Newly
introduced points could correspond to existing static structures or to static
points that were earlier obstructed by dynamic objects. To the best of our
knowledge, we are the first to use such a strategy for sparse LiDAR point
clouds. Existing solutions close to our approach fail to identify and preserve
the global static LiDAR topology and generate sub-optimal points. We propose
GLiDR, a Graph Generative network that is topologically regularized using
0-dimensional Persistent Homology ($\mathcal{PH}$) constraints. This enables
GLiDR to introduce newer static points along a topologically consistent global
static LiDAR backbone. GLiDR generates precise static points using $32\times$
sparser dynamic scans and performs better than the baselines across three
datasets. GLiDR generates a valuable byproduct - an accurate binary
segmentation mask of static and dynamic objects that are helpful for navigation
planning and safety in constrained environments. The newly introduced static
points allow GLiDR to outperform LiDAR-based navigation using SLAM in several
settings. Source code is available at https://kshitijbhat.github.io/glidr

search_paper_list.title:
Modeling Dense Multimodal Interactions Between Biological Pathways and
  Histology for Survival Prediction
search_paper_list.summary:
Integrating whole-slide images (WSIs) and bulk transcriptomics for predicting
patient survival can improve our understanding of patient prognosis. However,
this multimodal task is particularly challenging due to the different nature of
these data: WSIs represent a very high-dimensional spatial description of a
tumor, while bulk transcriptomics represent a global description of gene
expression levels within that tumor. In this context, our work aims to address
two key challenges: (1) how can we tokenize transcriptomics in a semantically
meaningful and interpretable way?, and (2) how can we capture dense multimodal
interactions between these two modalities? Specifically, we propose to learn
biological pathway tokens from transcriptomics that can encode specific
cellular functions. Together with histology patch tokens that encode the
different morphological patterns in the WSI, we argue that they form
appropriate reasoning units for downstream interpretability analyses. We
propose fusing both modalities using a memory-efficient multimodal Transformer
that can model interactions between pathway and histology patch tokens. Our
proposed model, SURVPATH, achieves state-of-the-art performance when evaluated
against both unimodal and multimodal baselines on five datasets from The Cancer
Genome Atlas. Our interpretability framework identifies key multimodal
prognostic factors, and, as such, can provide valuable insights into the
interaction between genotype and phenotype, enabling a deeper understanding of
the underlying biological mechanisms at play. We make our code public at:
https://github.com/ajv012/SurvPath.

search_paper_list.title:
Domain Adaptive Nuclei Instance Segmentation and Classification via
  Category-aware Feature Alignment and Pseudo-labelling
search_paper_list.summary:
Unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) methods have been broadly utilized to
improve the models' adaptation ability in general computer vision. However,
different from the natural images, there exist huge semantic gaps for the
nuclei from different categories in histopathology images. It is still
under-explored how could we build generalized UDA models for precise
segmentation or classification of nuclei instances across different datasets.
In this work, we propose a novel deep neural network, namely Category-Aware
feature alignment and Pseudo-Labelling Network (CAPL-Net) for UDA nuclei
instance segmentation and classification. Specifically, we first propose a
category-level feature alignment module with dynamic learnable trade-off
weights. Second, we propose to facilitate the model performance on the target
data via self-supervised training with pseudo labels based on nuclei-level
prototype features. Comprehensive experiments on cross-domain nuclei instance
segmentation and classification tasks demonstrate that our approach outperforms
state-of-the-art UDA methods with a remarkable margin.

search_paper_list.title:
Pathology-genomic fusion via biologically informed cross-modality graph
  learning for survival analysis
search_paper_list.summary:
The diagnosis and prognosis of cancer are typically based on multi-modal
clinical data, including histology images and genomic data, due to the complex
pathogenesis and high heterogeneity. Despite the advancements in digital
pathology and high-throughput genome sequencing, establishing effective
multi-modal fusion models for survival prediction and revealing the potential
association between histopathology and transcriptomics remains challenging. In
this paper, we propose Pathology-Genome Heterogeneous Graph (PGHG) that
integrates whole slide images (WSI) and bulk RNA-Seq expression data with
heterogeneous graph neural network for cancer survival analysis. The PGHG
consists of biological knowledge-guided representation learning network and
pathology-genome heterogeneous graph. The representation learning network
utilizes the biological prior knowledge of intra-modal and inter-modal data
associations to guide the feature extraction. The node features of each
modality are updated through attention-based graph learning strategy. Unimodal
features and bi-modal fused features are extracted via attention pooling module
and then used for survival prediction. We evaluate the model on low-grade
gliomas, glioblastoma, and kidney renal papillary cell carcinoma datasets from
the Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) and the First Affiliated Hospital of Zhengzhou
University (FAHZU). Extensive experimental results demonstrate that the
proposed method outperforms both unimodal and other multi-modal fusion models.
For demonstrating the model interpretability, we also visualize the attention
heatmap of pathological images and utilize integrated gradient algorithm to
identify important tissue structure, biological pathways and key genes.

search_paper_list.title:
Improving Coherence and Consistency in Neural Sequence Models with
  Dual-System, Neuro-Symbolic Reasoning
search_paper_list.summary:
Human reasoning can often be understood as an interplay between two systems:
the intuitive and associative ("System 1") and the deliberative and logical
("System 2"). Neural sequence models -- which have been increasingly successful
at performing complex, structured tasks -- exhibit the advantages and failure
modes of System 1: they are fast and learn patterns from data, but are often
inconsistent and incoherent. In this work, we seek a lightweight, training-free
means of improving existing System 1-like sequence models by adding System
2-inspired logical reasoning. We explore several variations on this theme in
which candidate generations from a neural sequence model are examined for
logical consistency by a symbolic reasoning module, which can either accept or
reject the generations. Our approach uses neural inference to mediate between
the neural System 1 and the logical System 2. Results in robust story
generation and grounded instruction-following show that this approach can
increase the coherence and accuracy of neurally-based generations.

search_paper_list.title:
Temporal Logic Specification-Conditioned Decision Transformer for
  Offline Safe Reinforcement Learning
search_paper_list.summary:
Offline safe reinforcement learning (RL) aims to train a constraint
satisfaction policy from a fixed dataset. Current state-of-the-art approaches
are based on supervised learning with a conditioned policy. However, these
approaches fall short in real-world applications that involve complex tasks
with rich temporal and logical structures. In this paper, we propose temporal
logic Specification-conditioned Decision Transformer (SDT), a novel framework
that harnesses the expressive power of signal temporal logic (STL) to specify
complex temporal rules that an agent should follow and the sequential modeling
capability of Decision Transformer (DT). Empirical evaluations on the DSRL
benchmarks demonstrate the better capacity of SDT in learning safe and
high-reward policies compared with existing approaches. In addition, SDT shows
good alignment with respect to different desired degrees of satisfaction of the
STL specification that it is conditioned on.

search_paper_list.title:
A Circuit Domain Generalization Framework for Efficient Logic Synthesis
  in Chip Design
search_paper_list.summary:
Logic Synthesis (LS) plays a vital role in chip design -- a cornerstone of
the semiconductor industry. A key task in LS is to transform circuits --
modeled by directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) -- into simplified circuits with
equivalent functionalities. To tackle this task, many LS operators apply
transformations to subgraphs -- rooted at each node on an input DAG --
sequentially. However, we found that a large number of transformations are
ineffective, which makes applying these operators highly time-consuming. In
particular, we notice that the runtime of the Resub and Mfs2 operators often
dominates the overall runtime of LS optimization processes. To address this
challenge, we propose a novel data-driven LS operator paradigm, namely PruneX,
to reduce ineffective transformations. The major challenge of developing PruneX
is to learn models that well generalize to unseen circuits, i.e., the
out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization problem. Thus, the major technical
contribution of PruneX is the novel circuit domain generalization framework,
which learns domain-invariant representations based on the
transformation-invariant domain-knowledge. To the best of our knowledge, PruneX
is the first approach to tackle the OOD problem in LS operators. We integrate
PruneX with the aforementioned Resub and Mfs2 operators. Experiments
demonstrate that PruneX significantly improves their efficiency while keeping
comparable optimization performance on industrial and very large-scale
circuits, achieving up to $3.1\times$ faster runtime.

In most of the stages in the workflow,recent studies have demonstrated significant improvementby using ML methods compared with traditional methods,including high-level synthesis [23], [24], [25], logic synthesis[1], [13], [26], and placement [18], [21], [22], [27], [28].In this paper, we focus on using machine learning to pro-mote efficient logic synthesis (LS), which plays a vital rolein efficient chip design and can yield substantial economicvalue [13], [29]. Existing research on machine learning forLS can be roughly divided into three categories [1], [17].First, [30], [31], [32], [33] use machine learning to tune theoptimization flow of LS operators. Second, [13], [34], [35]use machine learning to predict key metrics after physicaldesign and leverage the prediction to guide LS optimization.Third, [36], [37] use machine learning to improve decision-making in traditional LS methods. Different from existingwork, our work uses machine learning to improve theparadigm of traditional LS operators to promote efficient LS.An appealing feature of our PruneX is that it is applicable tomany LS operators—which follow the paradigm illustratedin Fig. 2—to significantly improve their efficiency.2.2 Generalizable Prediction in Chip Design WorkflowPrior research has investigated the utilization of machinelearning (ML) techniques to develop generalizable conges-tion prediction models within the chip design workflow[38], [39], [40], [41]. Nevertheless, our work differs fromprevious studies in two fundamental aspects. First, weaddress dissimilar input data. Prior research mainly focuseson the physical design stage with circuits represented bygate-level netlists or designed layouts, while we focus on thelogic synthesis stage with circuits represented by Booleannetworks. The dissimilarity in input data poses significantchallenges in directly applying their methods to our set-ting. To the best of our knowledge, our work is the firstdata-driven method to well tackle the out-of-distribution(OOD) generalization problem across circuits in LS oper-ators, which is critical for the success of data-driven LSalgorithms. Second, we employ different methodologies forlearning models. Generally, they propose problem-specificgraph neural network architectures and learn the modelsvia supervised learning. In contrast, our PruneX formulatesthe OOD generalization problem across circuits as a novelcircuit domain generalization task, which offers promisingavenues for future research on prediction tasks in chipdesign. Moreover, based on a key observation called thetransformation-invariant domain knowledge, our PruneXfurther proposes to learn domain-invariant representationsfor enhanced generalization capabilities.3 B ACKGROUND3.1 Logic Synthesis (LS)Driven by Moore’s law, the chip design complexity hasgrown exponentially [17], [18], [19], [42], [43]. Thus, the chipdesign workflow has incorporated multiple Electronic De-sign Automation (EDA) tools to synthesize, simulate, test,and verify different circuit designs efficiently and reliably.These EDA tools automatize the chip design workflow asshown in Fig. 1a. A LS tool—which aims to transform abehavioral description of a design into an optimized gate-level circuit implementation—is one of the most impor-tant modules in the EDA tools. In general, LS consists ofpre-mapping optimization, technology mapping, and post-mapping optimization [17], [44]. In this paper, we defineJOURNAL OF LATEX CLASS FILES, VOL. 14, NO. 8, AUGUST 2015 4Circuit Optimization (CO) by both pre-mapping opti-mization and post-mapping optimization. First, in the pre-mapping optimization phase, logic optimization operators,such as Rewrite [4], Resub [10], and Refactor [12], areapplied to an input circuit to optimize the circuit. Then, inthe technology mapping phase, the optimized logic circuit ismapped to the available technology library, e.g., a standard-cell netlist [45] or k-input lookup-tables [16]. Finally, post-mapping optimization operators, such as Mfs2 [9], are ap-plied to the mapped circuit to further optimize it.3.2 Circuit Optimization in LSCircuit Optimization (CO) in LS aims to transform an inputcircuit into a simplified circuit with equivalent functionalityand reduced size and/or depth. Thus, well tackling the COtask can significantly save the hardware resources requiredto design a specific chip [3]. As circuit representations inthe pre-mapping and post-mapping optimization phases aredifferent, we first discuss circuit representations in the twophases. Then, we provide details on LS operators.3.2.1 Circuit RepresentationIn the LS stage, a circuit is usually modeled by a Booleannetwork. In this paper, we use the terms Boolean networkand circuit interchangeably. A Boolean network is a di-rected acyclic graph (DAG), where nodes correspond toBoolean functions and directed edges correspond to wiresconnecting these functions. A Boolean function takes theform f : Bn → B, where B = {0, 1} denotes the Booleandomain. Given a node, its fanins are nodes connected byincoming edges of this node, and its fanouts are nodesconnected by outgoing edges of this node. The primaryinputs (PIs) are nodes with no fanin, and the primary outputs(POs) are nodes with no fanout. The size of a circuit denotesthe number of nodes in the DAG. Thedepth (level) of a circuitdenotes the maximal length of a path from a PI to a PO inthe DAG. The size and depth of a circuit are proxy metricsfor the area and delay of the circuit, respectively.Common types of DAGs for CO include And-InverterGraphs (AIGs) for pre-mapping optimization [4], [11] andK-Input Look-Up Tables (K-LUTs) for post-mapping opti-mization [9], [16]. In the pre-mapping optimization phase,an AIG is a DAG containing four types of nodes: theconstant, PIs, POs, and two-input And (And2) nodes. Agraph edge is either complemented or not. A complementededge indicates that the signal is complemented. In the post-mapping optimization phase, a K-LUT is a DAG with nodescorresponding to Look-Up Tables and directed edges corre-sponding to wires. A Look-Up Table in a K-LUT is a digitalmemory that implements the Boolean function of the node.3.2.2 Commonly Used LS OperatorsA rich set of LS operators have been developed to tacklethe CO task in the pre-mapping and post-mapping opti-mization phases [7]. In this paper, we focus on commonlyused LS operators on large-scale industrial circuits—thatis, the Resub [10], Mfs2 [9], Rewrite [4], and Refactor [12]operators—which often act as a bottleneck to the efficiencyof the LS optimization processes (see Section 4.2). We no-tice that these LS operators follow the same paradigmas shown in Fig. 2. Specifically, they apply transforma-tions to subgraphs rooted at each node—that is, the node-level transformation—sequentially for all nodes on an inputDAG. To address this challenge, we propose a noveldata-driven LS operator paradigm (see Fig. 2), namelyPruneX, which promotes efficient LS by significantly im-proving the efficiency of LS operators. The major challengeof developing PruneX is how to learn models that can wellgeneralize to unseen circuits, that is, the out-of-distribution(OOD) generalization problem across circuits in LS opera-tors. Thus, the major technical contribution of PruneX is thenovel circuit domain generalization (COG) framework (seeFig. 4), which is critical for the success of data-driven LSalgorithms. Thus, the training set con-sists of heterogeneous samples from several distributions,i.e., nodes from several different circuits. That is, we aregiven N similar and related distributions, and aim to gen-eralize to a similar but different test distribution. Regardingthe source of these circuits, each circuit may be a samplegiven N similar and related distributions, and aim to gen-eralize to a similar but different test distribution. Regardingthe source of these circuits, each circuit may be a sampleof a complex integrated circuit, such as an addition circuit,storage circuit, control circuit, etc. In addition, aggregatingcircuits with similar functionality is similar to samplingsome small building blocks from a complex integrated cir-cuit. Therefore, it is reasonable to assume that the trainingCircuit Domains and testing Circuit Domains come from thesame hyper-distribution. In general, we divide the real in-dustry setting into two categories. In the first category, weare given N circuits with their functionality information.In the second category, we are given N circuits withouttheir functionality information for privacy protection. In thefirst category, we aggregate those circuits with the samehigh-level functionality. Take the EPFL benchmark as anJOURNAL OF LATEX CLASS FILES, VOL. 14, NO. 8, AUGUST 2015 27example, we aggregate circuits with the arithmetic func-tionality and control functionality into an arithmetic CircuitDomain and a control Circuit Domain, respectively. Thus,the two Circuit Domains contain two large datasets withsimilar sample sizes, which is beneficial for achieving asmall generalization error bound. Moreover, the two CircuitDomains may come from small integrated units from acomplex integrated circuit, which follows Assumption 1.In the second category, we aggregate circuits to make thesample sizes across domains nearly uniform. Specifically, wesort the circuits according to their sample sizes, and dividethe odd-numbered circuits into one domain, and the even-numbered circuits into another domain. In this paper, weassume that the IWLS and industrial benchmarks fall intothe second category.D.6 Details of the Transformation-Invariant DomainKnowledgeHere we take the node-level transformation in the Resuband Mfs2 operators, i.e., the resubstitution transformation[10], as an example. The node-level transformations in theRewrite [4] and Refactor [12] operators are different frombut similar to the resubstitution transformation. Please referto [4] for details. In terms of the resubstitution transforma-tion, we are given a current node called the root node. Theresubstitution transformation first uses a heuristic rule tocollect a limited number of candidate input nodes of the rootnode. In general, the candidate input nodes include twotypes of nodes: (a) the nodes that are on the input directionof the root node and distance-m or less from the root node,and (b) the nodes that are on the output direction of thetype (a) nodes and with level not exceeding the level of theroot node. The resubstitution transformation focuses on thesubgraph constructed by the root node and candidate inputnodes. Next, the resubstitution transformation aims to find anew set of input nodes from candidate input nodes to replaceexisting input nodes of the current node without changing itsfunctionality, thereby reducing the size and/or depth of thecircuit.Thus, the resubstitution transformation mechanism is in-variant across different circuits. Moreover, whether a resub-stitution transformation can be effective is highly related tothe focused subgraph regardless of what the global graph is.Based on the transformation-invariant domain knowledge,we propose to extract the subgraph rooted at a node to learnits node embedding for discriminative classification, whichcarries the potential to learn domain-invariant representa-tions and thus well generalize to unseen circuits. As the Resub operatorand the Mfs2 operator are logic optimization and post-mapping optimization operators respectively, their corre-sponding input directed acyclic graphs are different. Forthe logic optimization operator Resub, the input circuit isusually represented as an And-Inverter Graph (AIG). Forthe post-mapping optimization operator Mfs2, the inputcircuit is represented as a k-inputs Look up tables (k-LUTs).Please refer to Section 3 for details on the AIG and k-LUTs.Therefore, for the two different types of operators, thespecific designed node features are slightly different. Specif-ically, for the Mfs2 operator, we design node features withthe truth table of the node (i.e., a 6-input look up table)and other possible useful features, such as the fanin/fanoutnumber and level of the node. Overall, the node feature forthe Mfs2 operator is a 69-dimensional vector. Moreover, forthe Resub operator, we consider features from the node itselfand from its two children to capture structural information,the Mfs2 operator is a 69-dimensional vector. Moreover, forthe Resub operator, we consider features from the node itselfand from its two children to capture structural information,which follows [36]. We use the two features inv0 and inv1 tocapture the functionality information, where inv0/inv1 = 1denotes that the left/right input edge is inverted. Thus, thenode feature consists of the root node feature (8-dimensionalvector) and its two children features (two 6-dimensionalvectors). Note that its children features do not contain thecut information, i.e., the Leaves number and Cuts number.Overall, the node feature for the Resub operator is a 20-dimensional vector.D.7.2 Implementation Details of PruneXAs shown in Fig. 2, our proposed PruneX first extract nodefeatures, i.e., constructing bipartite graphs for all nodes asmentioned in Section 5.2.2. PruneX then call the learnedclassifier to predict the score that a node is effective forall nodes. The learned classifier is operator-specific. That is,we learn an individual classifier for each given operator, asthe input circuit representation for different operators aredifferent and thus the designed node features are different.Note that an input circuit is modeled by a directed acylicgraph (DAG), and each node on the DAG has a uniqueidentification number (ID). Thus, PruneX sort the node IDsin descending order according to the scores, and select thetop k% node IDs. Finally, PruneX only applies node-leveltransformations in sequence to nodes in the selected nodeID set.The model inference time in PruneX is low, as PruneXonly needs to call the inference model once. However, theremay be a marginal shift between the predicted node IDsand the true node IDs. The reason is that when applyingnode-level transformations in sequence, the structure of thegraph may change. This causes the true node IDs to change,while the predicted node IDs are fixed. Fortunately, wefound that the shift between the predicted node IDs andthe true node IDs has marginal impact on the optimizationperformance of the operators for the following two reasons.First, the ID set of effective nodes is quite sparse due tothe ineffective node-level transformations problem. There-fore, the influence between consecutive effective node-leveltransformations is slight. For example, the Resub operator applies theresubstitution transformation. We provide details on theresubstitution transformation in Appendix D.6. As shownin Fig. 2 (Right), our PruneX uses a learned classifier topredict those nodes with effective node-level transforma-tions in advance, and applies node-level transformations tothese predicted effective nodes sequentially. Note that theparadigm of our PruneX is independent from the node-leveltransformations. Thus, our PruneX can also be applied to theRewrite and Refactor operators.D.7.4 Implementation Details of COGHardware Specification Throughout all experiments, weuse a single machine that contains eight GPU devices(Nvidia GeForce GTX 3090 Ti) and two Intel Gold 6246RCPUs.Neural Network Architecture The GCNN model encodesnode features into embeddings with dimension 128. Themulti-head neural network contains a shared multi-layerperceptron containing three hidden layers with 1024 unitswith M heads branching off independently. To output clas-sification probabilities for values between 0 and 1, the multi-head neural network uses a Sigmoid activation function atthe last layer.Training Details Throughout all experiments, we applyAdam optimizer with learning rate α = 1e − 4 to optimizeour models. Moreover, for training stability, we apply linearlearning rate decay with step size 100 and decay rate 0.96.For generalization to very large-scale circuits, we apply Min-Max Normalization to data in training and testing datasets.Due to limited video memory, we set the batch size to 10240.For simplicity, we train models for 3000 epochs, and save thethree models at 1000, 2000, and 3000 epochs. candidate_base_papers_info_list.title:
Modeling Dense Multimodal Interactions Between Biological Pathways and
  Histology for Survival Prediction
candidate_base_papers_info_list.summary:
Integrating whole-slide images (WSIs) and bulk transcriptomics for predicting
patient survival can improve our understanding of patient prognosis. However,
this multimodal task is particularly challenging due to the different nature of
these data: WSIs represent a very high-dimensional spatial description of a
tumor, while bulk transcriptomics represent a global description of gene
expression levels within that tumor. In this context, our work aims to address
two key challenges: (1) how can we tokenize transcriptomics in a semantically
meaningful and interpretable way?, and (2) how can we capture dense multimodal
interactions between these two modalities? Specifically, we propose to learn
biological pathway tokens from transcriptomics that can encode specific
cellular functions. Together with histology patch tokens that encode the
different morphological patterns in the WSI, we argue that they form
appropriate reasoning units for downstream interpretability analyses. We
propose fusing both modalities using a memory-efficient multimodal Transformer
that can model interactions between pathway and histology patch tokens. Our
proposed model, SURVPATH, achieves state-of-the-art performance when evaluated
against both unimodal and multimodal baselines on five datasets from The Cancer
Genome Atlas. Our interpretability framework identifies key multimodal
prognostic factors, and, as such, can provide valuable insights into the
interaction between genotype and phenotype, enabling a deeper understanding of
the underlying biological mechanisms at play. We make our code public at:
https://github.com/ajv012/SurvPath.
candidate_base_papers_info_list.main_contributions: The paper introduces SURVPATH, a novel multimodal framework for predicting patient survival by integrating whole-slide histology images and bulk transcriptomic data. The main contributions include a biologically interpretable tokenization of transcriptomics into pathway tokens and an efficient multimodal Transformer architecture that fuses these tokens with histology patch tokens. This approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on multiple TCGA cancer datasets while offering multi-level interpretability of the modality interactions.
candidate_base_papers_info_list.methodology: The method first tokenizes transcriptomics data using established biological pathways (from Reactome and MSigDB Hallmarks) to generate pathway tokens via a sparse MLP, and tokenizes whole-slide images into patch tokens using a pre-trained Swin Transformer model. These tokens are then fed into a customized Transformer that uses a sparse attention pattern (ignoring patch-to-patch interactions) to model dense interactions between pathways and image patches. A survival prediction head is used to estimate discrete hazard functions, and integrated gradients are applied for multi-level interpretability.
candidate_base_papers_info_list.experimental_setup: Experiments were conducted on five TCGA datasets (BLCA, BRCA, STAD, COADREAD, HNSC) evaluating disease-specific survival using 5-fold cross-validation with stratification. The evaluation metrics include concordance index (c-index) and Kaplan-Meier survival curves with logrank tests. The study also compares SURVPATH against several unimodal and multimodal baselines, and ablation studies were performed to verify the impact of tokenization granularity and fusion schemes.
candidate_base_papers_info_list.limitations: The paper notes some limitations including the challenge of robust feature selection given high-dimensional and heterogeneous data, the modest size of available datasets leading to potential overfitting, and that certain design choices (e.g., ignoring patch-to-patch interactions or using low-rank approximations like Nyström) may underperform. Additionally, while the interpretability framework provides qualitative insights, quantitative metrics for interpretability are not provided.
candidate_base_papers_info_list.future_research_directions: Future work could focus on developing quantitative interpretability metrics at the dataset level, further exploring effective modeling of patch-to-patch interactions, and improving scalability as gene numbers increase. In addition, investigating the identified multimodal biomarkers for prognostication and potential targeted therapies, as well as validating the findings in larger clinical studies, are promising directions.

candidate_base_papers_info_list.title:
Morphological Prototyping for Unsupervised Slide Representation Learning
  in Computational Pathology
candidate_base_papers_info_list.summary:
Representation learning of pathology whole-slide images (WSIs) has been has
primarily relied on weak supervision with Multiple Instance Learning (MIL).
However, the slide representations resulting from this approach are highly
tailored to specific clinical tasks, which limits their expressivity and
generalization, particularly in scenarios with limited data. Instead, we
hypothesize that morphological redundancy in tissue can be leveraged to build a
task-agnostic slide representation in an unsupervised fashion. To this end, we
introduce PANTHER, a prototype-based approach rooted in the Gaussian mixture
model that summarizes the set of WSI patches into a much smaller set of
morphological prototypes. Specifically, each patch is assumed to have been
generated from a mixture distribution, where each mixture component represents
a morphological exemplar. Utilizing the estimated mixture parameters, we then
construct a compact slide representation that can be readily used for a wide
range of downstream tasks. By performing an extensive evaluation of PANTHER on
subtyping and survival tasks using 13 datasets, we show that 1) PANTHER
outperforms or is on par with supervised MIL baselines and 2) the analysis of
morphological prototypes brings new qualitative and quantitative insights into
model interpretability.
candidate_base_papers_info_list.main_contributions: The paper introduces PANTHER, a novel unsupervised slide representation learning framework for computational pathology that leverages morphological redundancy in tissue using prototype-based aggregation. By modeling patch embeddings with a Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) and extracting a compact, concatenated representation, PANTHER effectively summarizes whole-slide images for diverse tasks such as cancer subtyping and survival prediction.
candidate_base_papers_info_list.methodology: PANTHER first decomposes whole-slide images into patches and employs a pre-trained feature extractor to obtain patch embeddings. It then models these embeddings with a GMM where each mixture component corresponds to a morphological prototype. The Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithm is used to estimate mixture probabilities, means, and covariances, which are concatenated to form the slide's final representation. A per-prototype nonlinear mapping (MLP) is applied for improved prediction and interpretability by isolating contributions from distinct visual concepts.
candidate_base_papers_info_list.experimental_setup: The authors evaluate PANTHER on several diagnostic and prognostic tasks including four subtyping challenges (e.g., EBRAINS brain tumor subtyping, NSCLC classification, prostate cancer grading) and survival prediction on TCGA and external cohorts (CPTAC, NLST). They compare against both unsupervised baselines (DeepSets, ProtoCounts, H2T, OT) and supervised MIL methods (ABMIL, TransMIL, DSMIL, AttnMISL, ILRA) using metrics such as balanced accuracy, weighted F1, Cohen’s kappa, and concordance index. Ablation studies are performed by varying the number of prototypes and feature extractors.
candidate_base_papers_info_list.limitations: A key limitation mentioned is the fixed choice of number of prototypes (e.g., C=16), which may lead to over- or under-clustering for certain cancer types. The reliance on a GMM with diagonal covariance may restrict the expressivity of the patch distribution model and the evaluation does not fully cover rare cancer cohorts with limited data.
candidate_base_papers_info_list.future_research_directions: Future work includes developing more expressive mixture models for capturing patch distributions, determining the optimal number of prototypes in a data-driven manner, extending evaluation to rare cancers with small sample sizes, and integrating improved interpretability and end-to-end learning strategies to further enhance the unsupervised slide representation framework.

selected_base_paper_info.title:
Modeling Dense Multimodal Interactions Between Biological Pathways and
  Histology for Survival Prediction
selected_base_paper_info.summary:
Integrating whole-slide images (WSIs) and bulk transcriptomics for predicting
patient survival can improve our understanding of patient prognosis. However,
this multimodal task is particularly challenging due to the different nature of
these data: WSIs represent a very high-dimensional spatial description of a
tumor, while bulk transcriptomics represent a global description of gene
expression levels within that tumor. In this context, our work aims to address
two key challenges: (1) how can we tokenize transcriptomics in a semantically
meaningful and interpretable way?, and (2) how can we capture dense multimodal
interactions between these two modalities? Specifically, we propose to learn
biological pathway tokens from transcriptomics that can encode specific
cellular functions. Together with histology patch tokens that encode the
different morphological patterns in the WSI, we argue that they form
appropriate reasoning units for downstream interpretability analyses. We
propose fusing both modalities using a memory-efficient multimodal Transformer
that can model interactions between pathway and histology patch tokens. Our
proposed model, SURVPATH, achieves state-of-the-art performance when evaluated
against both unimodal and multimodal baselines on five datasets from The Cancer
Genome Atlas. Our interpretability framework identifies key multimodal
prognostic factors, and, as such, can provide valuable insights into the
interaction between genotype and phenotype, enabling a deeper understanding of
the underlying biological mechanisms at play. We make our code public at:
https://github.com/ajv012/SurvPath.
selected_base_paper_info.main_contributions: The paper introduces SURVPATH, a novel multimodal framework for predicting patient survival by integrating whole-slide histology images and bulk transcriptomic data. The main contributions include a biologically interpretable tokenization of transcriptomics into pathway tokens and an efficient multimodal Transformer architecture that fuses these tokens with histology patch tokens. This approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on multiple TCGA cancer datasets while offering multi-level interpretability of the modality interactions.
selected_base_paper_info.methodology: The method first tokenizes transcriptomics data using established biological pathways (from Reactome and MSigDB Hallmarks) to generate pathway tokens via a sparse MLP, and tokenizes whole-slide images into patch tokens using a pre-trained Swin Transformer model. These tokens are then fed into a customized Transformer that uses a sparse attention pattern (ignoring patch-to-patch interactions) to model dense interactions between pathways and image patches. A survival prediction head is used to estimate discrete hazard functions, and integrated gradients are applied for multi-level interpretability.
selected_base_paper_info.experimental_setup: Experiments were conducted on five TCGA datasets (BLCA, BRCA, STAD, COADREAD, HNSC) evaluating disease-specific survival using 5-fold cross-validation with stratification. The evaluation metrics include concordance index (c-index) and Kaplan-Meier survival curves with logrank tests. The study also compares SURVPATH against several unimodal and multimodal baselines, and ablation studies were performed to verify the impact of tokenization granularity and fusion schemes.
selected_base_paper_info.limitations: The paper notes some limitations including the challenge of robust feature selection given high-dimensional and heterogeneous data, the modest size of available datasets leading to potential overfitting, and that certain design choices (e.g., ignoring patch-to-patch interactions or using low-rank approximations like Nyström) may underperform. Additionally, while the interpretability framework provides qualitative insights, quantitative metrics for interpretability are not provided.
selected_base_paper_info.future_research_directions: Future work could focus on developing quantitative interpretability metrics at the dataset level, further exploring effective modeling of patch-to-patch interactions, and improving scalability as gene numbers increase. In addition, investigating the identified multimodal biomarkers for prognostication and potential targeted therapies, as well as validating the findings in larger clinical studies, are promising directions.

candidate_add_papers_info_list.title:
Morphological Prototyping for Unsupervised Slide Representation Learning
  in Computational Pathology
candidate_add_papers_info_list.summary:
Representation learning of pathology whole-slide images (WSIs) has been has
primarily relied on weak supervision with Multiple Instance Learning (MIL).
However, the slide representations resulting from this approach are highly
tailored to specific clinical tasks, which limits their expressivity and
generalization, particularly in scenarios with limited data. Instead, we
hypothesize that morphological redundancy in tissue can be leveraged to build a
task-agnostic slide representation in an unsupervised fashion. To this end, we
introduce PANTHER, a prototype-based approach rooted in the Gaussian mixture
model that summarizes the set of WSI patches into a much smaller set of
morphological prototypes. Specifically, each patch is assumed to have been
generated from a mixture distribution, where each mixture component represents
a morphological exemplar. Utilizing the estimated mixture parameters, we then
construct a compact slide representation that can be readily used for a wide
range of downstream tasks. By performing an extensive evaluation of PANTHER on
subtyping and survival tasks using 13 datasets, we show that 1) PANTHER
outperforms or is on par with supervised MIL baselines and 2) the analysis of
morphological prototypes brings new qualitative and quantitative insights into
model interpretability.
candidate_add_papers_info_list.main_contributions: This work introduces PANTHER, the first prototype-based framework for unsupervised slide representation learning in computational pathology. It leverages morphological redundancy in tissue by summarizing patch embeddings into a small set of morphological prototypes via a Gaussian mixture model. The method achieves competitive performance against both supervised and unsupervised baselines on a variety of clinical tasks while offering enhanced interpretability.
candidate_add_papers_info_list.methodology: The approach extracts patch embeddings using a pretrained vision encoder and models their distribution with a Gaussian mixture model (GMM), where each component represents a distinct morphological prototype. The Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithm is used to estimate mixture parameters including prototype assignment probabilities, means, covariances, and mixture weights, which are then concatenated to form a fixed-length slide-level representation. This representation is further used with structured multilayer perceptrons or linear classifiers for various downstream tasks.
candidate_add_papers_info_list.experimental_setup: The method is evaluated on multiple tasks including subtyping (e.g., EBRAINS brain cancer subtyping with 30 and 12 classes, NSCLC on TCGA/CPTAC, and prostate cancer grading on PANDA) and survival prediction (e.g., on TCGA datasets such as BRCA, CRC, BLCA, UCEC, KIRC, LUAD with external tests on CPTAC and NLST). candidate_add_papers_info_list.limitations: A primary limitation is the use of a fixed number of prototypes (e.g., C = 16) for all tasks, which may lead to over- or under-clustering in certain cancer types. candidate_add_papers_info_list.future_research_directions: Future work includes developing more expressive mixture models for patch distributions, determining the optimal number of prototypes in a data-driven manner, and extending evaluation to rare cancer cohorts with limited sample sizes. candidate_add_papers_info_list.title:
A Circuit Domain Generalization Framework for Efficient Logic Synthesis
  in Chip Design
candidate_add_papers_info_list.summary:
Logic Synthesis (LS) plays a vital role in chip design -- a cornerstone of
the semiconductor industry. A key task in LS is to transform circuits --
modeled by directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) -- into simplified circuits with
equivalent functionalities. To tackle this task, many LS operators apply
transformations to subgraphs -- rooted at each node on an input DAG --
sequentially. However, we found that a large number of transformations are
ineffective, which makes applying these operators highly time-consuming. In
particular, we notice that the runtime of the Resub and Mfs2 operators often
dominates the overall runtime of LS optimization processes. To address this
challenge, we propose a novel data-driven LS operator paradigm, namely PruneX,
to reduce ineffective transformations. The major challenge of developing PruneX
is to learn models that well generalize to unseen circuits, i.e., the
out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization problem. Thus, the major technical
contribution of PruneX is the novel circuit domain generalization framework,
which learns domain-invariant representations based on the
transformation-invariant domain-knowledge. To the best of our knowledge, PruneX
is the first approach to tackle the OOD problem in LS operators. We integrate
PruneX with the aforementioned Resub and Mfs2 operators. Experiments
demonstrate that PruneX significantly improves their efficiency while keeping
comparable optimization performance on industrial and very large-scale
circuits, achieving up to $3.1\times$ faster runtime.
candidate_add_papers_info_list.main_contributions: The paper identifies inefficiencies in logic synthesis (LS) processes caused by a high number of ineffective node-level transformations in commonly used LS operators such as Mfs2, Resub, Rewrite, and Refactor. It introduces a novel data-driven framework called PruneX that integrates learned classifiers into the LS flow to predict and skip ineffective transformations. A key contribution is the formulation of circuit domain generalization (COG) that leverages transformation‐invariant domain knowledge to learn domain-invariant representations, allowing the approach to generalize well to unseen circuits.
candidate_add_papers_info_list.methodology: The proposed approach involves two main phases: an offline phase where training data is collected by applying LS operators to circuits and labeling nodes as effective or ineffective, and an online phase where the learned classifier predicts the most promising nodes for transformation. The method utilizes techniques such as focal loss to handle class imbalance, ensemble multilayer perceptrons (EnsembleMLP) as baselines, and a knowledge-driven subgraph representation (using a variant of graph convolutional neural networks) to extract domain-invariant features. It also introduces a domain-aware distributional classifier that adapts to circuits aggregated into multiple domains.
candidate_add_papers_info_list.experimental_setup: Experiments were conducted on multiple benchmarks including open-source datasets (EPFL and IWLS) and industrial circuits from Huawei HiSilicon, with circuits ranging from thousands to tens of millions of nodes. The evaluation involved standard LS operators (Mfs2, Resub, Rewrite, and Refactor) and used metrics such as top-k accuracy (recall), runtime improvement, as well as circuit size and depth as proxies for quality of synthesis. Two evaluation strategies were designed: leave-one-out cross-validation on circuits within a benchmark and cross-benchmark generalization tests to validate out-of-distribution performance.
candidate_add_papers_info_list.limitations: The approach relies on manually designed node features and the effectiveness of the learned models is constrained by class imbalance and distribution shifts between training and unseen circuits. Model inference time, although small relative to operator runtime, can become significant for very large-scale circuits if not parallelized. Moreover, there is sensitivity to the selection of hyperparameters (such as the percentage of nodes to transform) and assumptions regarding circuit aggregation that may not hold in all practical settings.
candidate_add_papers_info_list.future_research_directions: Potential future work includes extending the PruneX framework to other LS operators and further automating node feature extraction. Research could focus on improving model parallelism and inference efficiency for very large-scale circuits, exploring alternative domain generalization techniques and architectures, and investigating methods to further mitigate class imbalance issues. Additionally, refining the circuit aggregation mechanism and incorporating more detailed functionality information could improve generalization and optimization performance.

candidate_add_papers_info_list.title:
Modeling Dense Multimodal Interactions Between Biological Pathways and
  Histology for Survival Prediction
candidate_add_papers_info_list.summary:
Integrating whole-slide images (WSIs) and bulk transcriptomics for predicting
patient survival can improve our understanding of patient prognosis. However,
this multimodal task is particularly challenging due to the different nature of
these data: WSIs represent a very high-dimensional spatial description of a
tumor, while bulk transcriptomics represent a global description of gene
expression levels within that tumor. In this context, our work aims to address
two key challenges: (1) how can we tokenize transcriptomics in a semantically
meaningful and interpretable way?, and (2) how can we capture dense multimodal
interactions between these two modalities? Specifically, we propose to learn
biological pathway tokens from transcriptomics that can encode specific
cellular functions. Together with histology patch tokens that encode the
different morphological patterns in the WSI, we argue that they form
appropriate reasoning units for downstream interpretability analyses. We
propose fusing both modalities using a memory-efficient multimodal Transformer
that can model interactions between pathway and histology patch tokens. Our
proposed model, SURVPATH, achieves state-of-the-art performance when evaluated
against both unimodal and multimodal baselines on five datasets from The Cancer
Genome Atlas. Our interpretability framework identifies key multimodal
prognostic factors, and, as such, can provide valuable insights into the
interaction between genotype and phenotype, enabling a deeper understanding of
the underlying biological mechanisms at play. We make our code public at:
https://github.com/ajv012/SurvPath.
candidate_add_papers_info_list.main_contributions: The paper introduces SURVPATH, a novel multimodal Transformer model that integrates transcriptomics and histology for patient survival prediction. It proposes a new transcriptomics tokenization scheme based on biological pathway definitions and a memory‐efficient fusion mechanism that models dense cross-modal interactions, achieving state-of-the-art performance on diverse TCGA datasets.
candidate_add_papers_info_list.methodology: Transcriptomics data is tokenized into biologically meaningful pathway tokens using a sparse multi-layer perceptron guided by Reactome and MSigDB pathway definitions. Histology whole-slide images are decomposed into patch tokens via a pre-trained Swin Transformer. These tokens are fused early in a customized multimodal Transformer that employs a sparse attention mechanism (ignoring patch-to-patch interactions) to efficiently model dense interactions between modalities.
candidate_add_papers_info_list.experimental_setup: The method is evaluated on five TCGA datasets (BLCA, BRCA, STAD, COADREAD, and HNSC) using 5-fold cross-validation. Performance is measured using the concordance index (c-index) and Kaplan-Meier survival curves, and results are compared with various unimodal and multimodal baselines as well as clinical covariate models.
candidate_add_papers_info_list.limitations: Key limitations include reliance on predefined biological pathway groupings, limited exploration of patch-to-patch interactions (which did not improve performance), potential overfitting due to relatively small dataset sizes, and the primarily qualitative nature of the interpretability framework.
candidate_add_papers_info_list.future_research_directions: Future directions could include developing quantitative interpretability metrics at a dataset level, investigating more effective strategies for modeling patch-to-patch interactions, extending the tokenization approach to larger or more diverse gene sets, and incorporating additional modalities or clinical variables to further improve survival prediction.

candidate_add_papers_info_list.title:
A Circuit Domain Generalization Framework for Efficient Logic Synthesis
  in Chip Design
candidate_add_papers_info_list.summary:
Logic Synthesis (LS) plays a vital role in chip design -- a cornerstone of
the semiconductor industry. A key task in LS is to transform circuits --
modeled by directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) -- into simplified circuits with
equivalent functionalities. To tackle this task, many LS operators apply
transformations to subgraphs -- rooted at each node on an input DAG --
sequentially. However, we found that a large number of transformations are
ineffective, which makes applying these operators highly time-consuming. In
particular, we notice that the runtime of the Resub and Mfs2 operators often
dominates the overall runtime of LS optimization processes. To address this
challenge, we propose a novel data-driven LS operator paradigm, namely PruneX,
to reduce ineffective transformations. The major challenge of developing PruneX
is to learn models that well generalize to unseen circuits, i.e., the
out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization problem. Thus, the major technical
contribution of PruneX is the novel circuit domain generalization framework,
which learns domain-invariant representations based on the
transformation-invariant domain-knowledge. To the best of our knowledge, PruneX
is the first approach to tackle the OOD problem in LS operators. We integrate
PruneX with the aforementioned Resub and Mfs2 operators. Experiments
demonstrate that PruneX significantly improves their efficiency while keeping
comparable optimization performance on industrial and very large-scale
circuits, achieving up to $3.1\times$ faster runtime.
candidate_add_papers_info_list.main_contributions: The paper identifies inefficiencies in logic synthesis (LS) processes caused by a high number of ineffective node-level transformations in commonly used LS operators such as Mfs2, Resub, Rewrite, and Refactor. It introduces a novel data-driven framework called PruneX that integrates learned classifiers into the LS flow to predict and skip ineffective transformations. A key contribution is the formulation of circuit domain generalization (COG) that leverages transformation‐invariant domain knowledge to learn domain-invariant representations, allowing the approach to generalize well to unseen circuits.
candidate_add_papers_info_list.methodology: The proposed approach involves two main phases: an offline phase where training data is collected by applying LS operators to circuits and labeling nodes as effective or ineffective, and an online phase where the learned classifier predicts the most promising nodes for transformation. The method utilizes techniques such as focal loss to handle class imbalance, ensemble multilayer perceptrons (EnsembleMLP) as baselines, and a knowledge-driven subgraph representation (using a variant of graph convolutional neural networks) to extract domain-invariant features. It also introduces a domain-aware distributional classifier that adapts to circuits aggregated into multiple domains.
candidate_add_papers_info_list.experimental_setup: Experiments were conducted on multiple benchmarks including open-source datasets (EPFL and IWLS) and industrial circuits from Huawei HiSilicon, with circuits ranging from thousands to tens of millions of nodes. The evaluation involved standard LS operators (Mfs2, Resub, Rewrite, and Refactor) and used metrics such as top-k accuracy (recall), runtime improvement, as well as circuit size and depth as proxies for quality of synthesis. Two evaluation strategies were designed: leave-one-out cross-validation on circuits within a benchmark and cross-benchmark generalization tests to validate out-of-distribution performance.
candidate_add_papers_info_list.limitations: The approach relies on manually designed node features and the effectiveness of the learned models is constrained by class imbalance and distribution shifts between training and unseen circuits. Model inference time, although small relative to operator runtime, can become significant for very large-scale circuits if not parallelized. Moreover, there is sensitivity to the selection of hyperparameters (such as the percentage of nodes to transform) and assumptions regarding circuit aggregation that may not hold in all practical settings.
candidate_add_papers_info_list.future_research_directions: Potential future work includes extending the PruneX framework to other LS operators and further automating node feature extraction. Research could focus on improving model parallelism and inference efficiency for very large-scale circuits, exploring alternative domain generalization techniques and architectures, and investigating methods to further mitigate class imbalance issues. Additionally, refining the circuit aggregation mechanism and incorporating more detailed functionality information could improve generalization and optimization performance.

selected_add_paper_info_list.title:
Morphological Prototyping for Unsupervised Slide Representation Learning
  in Computational Pathology
selected_add_paper_info_list.summary:
Representation learning of pathology whole-slide images (WSIs) has been has
primarily relied on weak supervision with Multiple Instance Learning (MIL).
However, the slide representations resulting from this approach are highly
tailored to specific clinical tasks, which limits their expressivity and
generalization, particularly in scenarios with limited data. Instead, we
hypothesize that morphological redundancy in tissue can be leveraged to build a
task-agnostic slide representation in an unsupervised fashion. To this end, we
introduce PANTHER, a prototype-based approach rooted in the Gaussian mixture
model that summarizes the set of WSI patches into a much smaller set of
morphological prototypes. Specifically, each patch is assumed to have been
generated from a mixture distribution, where each mixture component represents
a morphological exemplar. Utilizing the estimated mixture parameters, we then
construct a compact slide representation that can be readily used for a wide
range of downstream tasks. By performing an extensive evaluation of PANTHER on
subtyping and survival tasks using 13 datasets, we show that 1) PANTHER
outperforms or is on par with supervised MIL baselines and 2) the analysis of
morphological prototypes brings new qualitative and quantitative insights into
model interpretability.
selected_add_paper_info_list.main_contributions: This work introduces PANTHER, the first prototype-based framework for unsupervised slide representation learning in computational pathology. It leverages morphological redundancy in tissue by summarizing patch embeddings into a small set of morphological prototypes via a Gaussian mixture model. The method achieves competitive performance against both supervised and unsupervised baselines on a variety of clinical tasks while offering enhanced interpretability.
selected_add_paper_info_list.methodology: The approach extracts patch embeddings using a pretrained vision encoder and models their distribution with a Gaussian mixture model (GMM), where each component represents a distinct morphological prototype. The Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithm is used to estimate mixture parameters including prototype assignment probabilities, means, covariances, and mixture weights, which are then concatenated to form a fixed-length slide-level representation. This representation is further used with structured multilayer perceptrons or linear classifiers for various downstream tasks.
selected_add_paper_info_list.experimental_setup: The method is evaluated on multiple tasks including subtyping (e.g., EBRAINS brain cancer subtyping with 30 and 12 classes, NSCLC on TCGA/CPTAC, and prostate cancer grading on PANDA) and survival prediction (e.g., on TCGA datasets such as BRCA, CRC, BLCA, UCEC, KIRC, LUAD with external tests on CPTAC and NLST). Results are benchmarked against several unsupervised methods (DeepSets, ProtoCounts, H2T, OT) and supervised MIL baselines (ABMIL, TransMIL, DSMIL, AttnMISL, ILRA) using metrics such as balanced accuracy, F1 score, Cohen’s κ, and concordance index (c-index).
selected_add_paper_info_list.limitations: A primary limitation is the use of a fixed number of prototypes (e.g., C = 16) for all tasks, which may lead to over- or under-clustering in certain cancer types. Additionally, while the unsupervised approach provides robust representations, it may require further adaptation to handle varied tissue morphologies and different dataset characteristics.
selected_add_paper_info_list.future_research_directions: Future work includes developing more expressive mixture models for patch distributions, determining the optimal number of prototypes in a data-driven manner, and extending evaluation to rare cancer cohorts with limited sample sizes. Additional research could also explore integrating multi-modal data and further enhancing the interpretability of the learned representations.

Below is the outcome of step 3—a truly new method inspired by both the Base Method and the selected Add Method (PANTHER):

Proposed Method: ProtoSurvPath

Overview:
ProtoSurvPath is a unified, prototype-based multimodal framework for survival prediction in oncology that simultaneously learns compact, data-driven representations for both transcriptomics and whole-slide histology images. By bridging the Base Method’s biologically informed tokenization with the unsupervised, prototype‐based summarization of PANTHER, ProtoSurvPath addresses issues of overfitting, limited data size, and potential biases from fixed prior knowledge while also capturing rich modality-specific redundancies and interactions.

Key Components:

1. Data-Driven Transcriptomic Prototyping:
 • Instead of exclusively relying on predefined biological pathways, ProtoSurvPath first encodes the bulk transcriptomic data via a dedicated gene expression encoder.
 • An unsupervised Gaussian mixture model (or a more expressive variant) is applied over the encoded gene profiles. The model clusters patient-specific gene expression patterns into a set of transcriptomic prototypes.
 • These prototypes capture latent biological states and activation modes across samples that may not be fully represented by existing pathway definitions, while also reducing the high dimensionality of transcriptomics.

2. Morphological Prototyping for Histology:
 • In parallel, whole-slide image patches are embedded using a pretrained vision encoder (e.g., a Swin Transformer or similar backbone).
 • Similar to PANTHER, a Gaussian mixture model is then applied on these patch embeddings to obtain a compact set of morphological prototypes that summarize the redundant patterns in tissue morphology.
 • By summarizing dozens or hundreds of patch tokens into a handful of morphological prototypes, the method mitigates noise, reduces computational overhead, and enhances generalization in the face of limited samples.

3. Cross-Modal Prototype Fusion:
 • The core of ProtoSurvPath is a multimodal fusion module that explicitly models interactions between the transcriptomic and morphological prototypes.
 • A lightweight, cross-attention Transformer architecture is designed to learn dense interactions between the two prototype sets. Unlike the Base Method’s fixed token–token interactions (which ignored patch-to-patch relations), this component allows the network to match molecular states with corresponding morphological patterns.
 • The attention maps produced by the Transformer provide a biologically grounded interpretability: clinicians and researchers can visualize which transcriptomic prototypes most strongly interact with specific morphological prototypes, revealing novel genotype–phenotype associations.

4. Advantages and Innovations:
 • Removing the sole reliance on established pathways introduces flexibility: the transcriptomic clustering process discovers latent, disease-specific biomarkers that may be missed by preset pathways.
 • Summarizing both modalities via unsupervised clustering drastically reduces the token count, helping to ease memory and computational burdens while improving the robustness of the fusion due to reduced noise.
 • The fusion module’s integrated attention over prototypes yields richer, more interpretable interactions. This not only has the potential to improve survival prediction accuracy but also provides actionable insights into underlying biological mechanisms.
 • By operating on compact, prototype-level representations rather than exhaustive, high-dimensional tokens, the framework is better suited for clinical scenarios with modest-sized datasets, thereby mitigating overfitting risks.

5. Implementation and Interpretability:
 • The framework begins with modality-specific encoders (a gene expression encoder for transcriptomics, a vision encoder for histology) followed by distinct yet analogous prototype extraction pipelines.
 • The transformer-based fusion module takes the concatenated prototype sets and outputs a survival risk score.
 • For transparency, integrated gradients or prototype assignment maps are computed over the cross-attention outputs, helping highlight the key interactions that drive the risk prediction.

In summary, ProtoSurvPath represents a significant evolution over the Base Method by leveraging unsupervised, prototype-based representation learning in both biological and histological domains. This dual prototyping strategy not only addresses the issues of limited dataset size and overfitting but also offers deeper, data-driven insights into the complex interplay between tumor morphology and gene expression.

1. Performance Comparison with Baselines

Goal:

Experimental Steps:

  • Use a publicly available oncology dataset such as a subset from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) with both transcriptomic (gene expression) and whole-slide imaging (WSI) data.
  • Preprocess the gene expression data (normalization, log-transformation) and extract patches/features from the WSIs (using an existing segmentation/detection model or patch extraction library).

 b. Model Architecture:
  • Construct the ProtoSurvPath neural network in PyTorch featuring:
   – A transcriptomic encoder (taking pathway-level features or a gene expression vector), for example, a simple feed-forward network.
   – A vision encoder (which extracts representations from image patches) that could use an off-the-shelf CNN (like ResNet pretrained on ImageNet) for feature extraction.
   – A cross-attention fusion module to integrate the two modalities.
   – A final survival analysis layer (for example, use a Cox proportional hazards loss or a ranking loss).
  • Implement baseline methods with similar modules except that they do not do dual prototyping. For instance:
   – “Base Method”: A single-stream network using concatenated features (transcriptomic + vision).
   – “PANTHER”: Another fusion method based on pre-defined biological priors.

 c. Clustering for Prototyping:
  • Utilize scikit-learn’s GaussianMixture for clustering pathway features (for transcriptomics) and for grouping patch embeddings (for morphology), thus producing prototypes.
  • The prototypes (cluster centers) serve to reduce token noise and are used in the cross-attention module.

 d. Training and Evaluation:
  • Split the TCGA dataset into training, validation, and test sets using scikit-learn’s model_selection module (e.g., StratifiedKFold or a standard train-test split).
  • For each method (ProtoSurvPath, Base Method, and PANTHER), train the model for the same number of epochs, tune hyperparameters, and use early stopping based on validation performance.
  • Evaluate survival prediction performance using the c-index (available from lifelines or custom evaluation functions) and time-dependent AUC.
  • Cross-validation: Repeat experiments across several folds and compute average performance.
  • Use paired statistical tests (e.g., paired t-tests) between methods’ results across cross-validation folds to assess significance.

Example Code Snippet for Training Loop (ProtoSurvPath):

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.optim as optim
from torch.utils.data import DataLoader
from sklearn.mixture import GaussianMixture
from sklearn.model_selection import KFold
import numpy as np

# Example dummy dataset class
class TCGADataset(torch.utils.data.Dataset):
    def __init__(self, gene_data, image_data, survival_time, event):
        self.gene_data = gene_data  # shape: [num_samples, num_genes]
        self.image_data = image_data  # shape: [num_samples, num_channels, H, W]
        self.survival_time = survival_time
        self.event = event
    def __len__(self):
        return len(self.survival_time)
    def __getitem__(self, idx):
        return {
            'gene': torch.tensor(self.gene_data[idx], dtype=torch.float),
            'image': torch.tensor(self.image_data[idx], dtype=torch.float),
            'time': self.survival_time[idx],
            'event': self.event[idx]
        }

# Dummy proto-survival model components
class GeneExpressionEncoder(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, input_dim, hidden_dim):
        super().__init__()
        self.encoder = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(input_dim, hidden_dim),
            nn.ReLU(),
            nn.Linear(hidden_dim, hidden_dim)
        )
    def forward(self, x):
        return self.encoder(x)

class VisionEncoder(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, num_channels, hidden_dim):
        super().__init__()
        self.encoder = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Conv2d(num_channels, 16, kernel_size=3, stride=1, padding=1),
            nn.BatchNorm2d(16),
            nn.ReLU(),
            nn.AdaptiveAvgPool2d((1,1))
        )
        self.fc = nn.Linear(16, hidden_dim)
    def forward(self, x):
        x = self.encoder(x)
        x = x.view(x.size(0), -1)
        return self.fc(x)

class CrossAttentionFusion(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, hidden_dim):
        super().__init__()
        self.query = nn.Linear(hidden_dim, hidden_dim)
        self.key = nn.Linear(hidden_dim, hidden_dim)
        self.value = nn.Linear(hidden_dim, hidden_dim)
        self.softmax = nn.Softmax(dim=-1)
    def forward(self, gene_feat, image_feat):
        Q = self.query(gene_feat)  # [batch, hidden_dim]
        K = self.key(image_feat)   # [batch, hidden_dim]
        V = self.value(image_feat)  # [batch, hidden_dim]
        attn_weights = self.softmax(torch.bmm(Q.unsqueeze(1), K.unsqueeze(2)))  # [batch, 1, 1]
        fused = attn_weights.squeeze() * V + gene_feat  # simple residual fusion for demo
        return fused

class ProtoSurvPath(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, gene_input_dim, image_channels, hidden_dim):
        super().__init__()
        self.gene_encoder = GeneExpressionEncoder(gene_input_dim, hidden_dim)
        self.vision_encoder = VisionEncoder(image_channels, hidden_dim)
        self.fusion = CrossAttentionFusion(hidden_dim)
        self.output = nn.Linear(hidden_dim, 1)  # risk score prediction, for Cox loss
    def forward(self, gene, image):
        gene_feat = self.gene_encoder(gene)
        image_feat = self.vision_encoder(image)
        fused_feat = self.fusion(gene_feat, image_feat)
        risk = self.output(fused_feat)
        return risk

# Assume we have our data loaded in gene_data, image_data, survival_time, event arrays
# Instantiate dataset, model, and optimizer
dataset = TCGADataset(gene_data=np.random.rand(100, 500),  # 500 genes
                      image_data=np.random.rand(100, 3, 224, 224),
                      survival_time=np.random.rand(100),
                      event=np.random.randint(0,2,100))
dataloader = DataLoader(dataset, batch_size=16, shuffle=True)

model = ProtoSurvPath(gene_input_dim=500, image_channels=3, hidden_dim=128)
optimizer = optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3)

# Dummy training loop (without actual survival loss for brevity)
for epoch in range(10):
    model.train()
    total_loss = 0.0
    for batch in dataloader:
        optimizer.zero_grad()
        risk = model(batch['gene'], batch['image'])
        # Here add survival loss computation (e.g., negative partial log likelihood for Cox model)
        loss = risk.mean()  # dummy loss
        loss.backward()
        optimizer.step()
        total_loss += loss.item()
    print(f"Epoch {epoch+1}, Loss: {total_loss/len(dataloader)}")

Expected Outcome:
 ProtoSurvPath should demonstrate higher prediction accuracy (c-index) and reliability, particularly when training data is limited, due to its noise reduction via prototyping and its dual-modality integration.

──────────────────────────────
2. Ablation Study of Prototype Extraction and Fusion Components

Goal:
 Assess the contribution of each component (transcriptomic prototyping, morphological prototyping, and the cross-attention fusion module) to the overall performance.

Experimental Steps:
 a. Create Variants:

  • Variant B: Remove morphological prototyping. Instead of applying Gaussian Mixture clustering on image embeddings, use all patch embeddings (or fixed image features) with the transcriptomic prototyping still in place.

# ---------------------------

class GeneExpressionEncoder(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, input_dim, hidden_dim):

            nn.Linear(input_dim, hidden_dim),
            nn.ReLU(),

        )
